subtitle: You've decided to risk 1% per trade. Now you need to translate that into actual contract counts on the exchange. This is the math that separates traders who say "I follow the 1% rule" from those who actually do.

blocks.content:
Lesson 6 covered why 1-2% risk is the survival rule. This lesson covers the arithmetic that turns that rule into actual contract counts. Without doing this math correctly, you're just guessing — and your "1% risk" trades end up being 3% or 5% in reality.

The good news: the formula is one line. The bad news: most traders never apply it.
The formula

blocks.title: Position size formula
blocks.content:
Position size (notional) = (equity × risk%) / (SL distance %)

Or in dollar terms:

Position size (notional) = $risk per trade / (SL distance %)

Where:

  • $risk per trade = the dollar amount you're willing to lose if SL hits (e.g., 1% of $1,000 account = $10)
  • SL distance % = the price distance from entry to SL, as a percentage of entry price (e.g., entry $60,000, SL $58,800 = 2.0% SL distance)
Worked example 1 — basic

Setup:

  • Account equity: $1,000
  • Risk rule: 1% per trade → $10 risk
  • Entry: $60,000 (long BTC)
  • Stop loss: $58,800
  • SL distance: ($60,000 − $58,800) / $60,000 = 2.0%

Calculation:

  • Position size = $10 / 2.0% = $500 notional
  • BTC quantity = $500 / $60,000 = 0.00833 BTC

Verification: If SL hits at $58,800, loss = 0.00833 BTC × ($60,000 − $58,800) = 0.00833 × $1,200 = $10. ✓ Exactly 1% of the $1,000 account.
Worked example 2 — tight SL = bigger notional

Setup:

  • Same $1,000 account, $10 risk
  • Entry: $60,000 (long BTC)
  • Tight SL at $59,400 (just below a key level)
  • SL distance: 1.0%

Calculation:

  • Position size = $10 / 1.0% = $1,000 notional
  • BTC quantity = $1,000 / $60,000 = 0.01667 BTC

Same dollar risk, but bigger position because the SL is tighter. This is the magic: tight stops let you size bigger without increasing risk. Why traders love good levels — close SL means same risk in dollars, bigger notional, bigger upside if it works.
Worked example 3 — wide SL = smaller notional

Setup:

  • Same account, same risk
  • Entry: $60,000
  • Wide SL at $57,000 (giving the trade more room)
  • SL distance: 5.0%

Calculation:

  • Position size = $10 / 5.0% = $200 notional
  • BTC quantity = $200 / $60,000 = 0.00333 BTC

Wider SL = smaller position to keep dollar risk constant. The trade-off: smaller upside if it works. But the math demands it.

blocks.title: Common mistake: thinking 'leverage = risk'
blocks.content:
Many traders pick leverage based on emotion ("10x feels right") instead of math. The right approach: compute the NOTIONAL position size needed for your risk + SL math, THEN figure out what leverage gets you there given your margin.

In Worked Example 1, notional = $500 on a $1,000 account = effective 0.5× leverage. Margin requirement is tiny. You could put it on at 1× and use $500 margin, or 10× and use $50 margin. Same notional, same dollar risk, same SL — the leverage number is just margin efficiency.

What matters: the notional and the SL distance. Leverage is downstream.
The contract-count quirk on perpetuals
On perpetuals, your position is denominated in contracts (or in coin quantity, depending on the exchange). The arithmetic is the same but the units differ.

rows: Compute notional in USDT, place that quantity
Compute notional → divide by current price → that's quantity in coin
Each contract = $1 or fixed coin amount

blocks.content: Read your exchange's docs ONCE to know which convention. After that, the math is the same. Most modern crypto exchanges use USDT-notional, which is the easiest.
Real-time check — "am I sizing right?"

Before clicking Buy, run this mental check:

  1. Where's my SL? Already decided, not negotiable.
  2. What's the % distance to SL from entry? Calculate it.
  3. What's 1% of my account in dollars? Cap on risk.
  4. Is my notional ≤ (dollars at risk / SL%)? If yes, size is fine. If no, REDUCE size until it is.

This check takes 15 seconds. It catches 90% of sizing errors. Most traders skip it because they're chasing the entry. That's exactly when you make the most expensive errors.
When you can't size to 1% — what to do

Two failure modes:

SL too far to size meaningfully: Your account is $300, 1% risk = $3, the setup has a 5% SL distance, so notional = $60. The minimum order size on the exchange might be $100. You can't take this trade at proper sizing. Options:

  • Skip the trade. The SL is too wide for your account size.
  • Wait for a tighter entry that lets a smaller SL distance fit your sizing.
  • Use a venue with smaller minimum order sizes.

Minimum size too large: Same scenario as above. The market is telling you your account is too small for THIS setup. Don't break sizing rules — find different setups (with tighter SL) or grow the account first.

blocks.title: Never size up because 'the min is bigger than my risk'
blocks.content:
Common rationalization: "the minimum order is $100 but my 1% risk only sizes to $60. Whatever, I'll just take the $100 trade." That's a 67% sizing increase. Your 1% risk becomes 1.67% on that trade. Across a year of this, your effective risk crosses into 3-5% territory and the math stops working.

The right answer: this setup isn't appropriate for your current account size. Skip it. Find ones that fit.
Scaling — when account grows, sizes grow
The 1% rule is on CURRENT equity, not starting equity. Update your dollar risk every time you trade.

Dollar risk scales with equity. Don't keep risking $10 when your account is $50,000 — that's now 0.02% risk, missing the growth opportunity. Don't keep risking $500 when your account drops to $10,000 — that's now 5%, breaking the survival rule.

blocks.title: Take this with you
blocks.content:
The formula: notional = (equity × risk%) / SL distance %

Memorize it. Apply it before every trade. The 15 seconds you spend doing this math is the difference between a trader who has a system and one who's just gambling with discipline-sounding language.

The journal you're using has a position-size widget on the Live Trade page — punch in equity, SL price, entry, and risk%, and it tells you the contract count. Use it. Don't trust your in-head math during a hot entry.
